opus-5.5.text:
I think informatics competitions were probably the single most formative thing in my teenage years, though not quite in the way people usually assume.

On the surface, it was about algorithms: learning dynamic programming, graph theory, data structures, and solving problems under time pressure. That training was real, and it still shapes how I think. When I face a messy problem today, my instinct is to strip it down, find the core structure, and ask what the simplest correct solution looks like. That habit came directly from hours of staring at problems I couldn't solve.

But the deeper influence was on my relationship with difficulty. In competitions you fail constantly. You read a problem, you have no idea, you try something, it's wrong, you get a time-limit error, you find a bug at the last minute or you don't. Over years, you learn that being stuck is a normal state, not a sign that you're not good enough. That emotional resilience, being comfortable not knowing for a long time, turned out to matter more than any specific algorithm.

The second thing was the people. Competitions put me in a community of extremely sharp, slightly obsessive young people. Many of them are still my closest friends, and many are now doing remarkable things in research, startups, and AI. Being surrounded by people like that at sixteen recalibrates your sense of what's possible. You stop thinking of ambitious things as something other people do.

I'd add one honest caveat. Competitions also have a narrowing effect. They reward speed, precision, and well-defined problems with a single correct answer. The real world, especially research or building a company, is mostly about choosing which problem to work on, and nobody gives you a test case for that. So part of my growth afterwards was unlearning some competition instincts: learning to tolerate ambiguity, to care about taste and direction, not just execution.

So I'd say competitions gave me the foundation: rigor, resilience, and a peer group. Everything after that was about figuring out what to build on top of it.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, informatics competitions were the first thing in my life that made me feel like I was good at something on my own terms. I started doing them in middle school, and at the beginning it wasn't about any grand ambition. It was just that I liked the feeling of a problem resisting me and then giving way. You sit there for hours, you're wrong forty times, and then suddenly the structure of the thing clicks and the code is almost trivial to write after that. That feeling is addictive, and I think it rewired how I approach everything.

The second thing it gave me was a very honest relationship with failure. In a contest, there's no partial credit for sounding smart. Your solution either passes or it doesn't, and the judge doesn't care how confident you felt. I lost a lot. I missed selections I thought I deserved. And looking back, that was probably more valuable than the wins, because it taught me to separate my ego from the result and to actually go look at where my thinking broke down.

And then there's the people. The community around these competitions is small and intense, and a lot of my closest friends and later collaborators came out of it. Many of the people I ended up working with, I first met in a training camp when we were sixteen and arguing about whether some problem was really a DP or a greedy in disguise.

I'll say one more thing, which is that it also had a cost. For a long time I thought the competition mindset was the only way to be smart, and it took me a while to understand that research, building products, leading a team, these reward different things. Patience, taste, tolerance for ambiguity. So competitions gave me the foundation, but a lot of my twenties was learning what they didn't teach me.

astra-6.text:
I’d say the biggest influence was learning how to approach a problem when the answer isn’t obvious. In an informatics competition, you have to turn an idea into something precise, test it, and figure out why it fails. That way of thinking can stay with you well beyond programming.

There’s also a useful lesson in getting stuck: it doesn’t necessarily mean you’re incapable. Sometimes you need a different perspective, or you need to break the problem into smaller pieces. So I see the value less in the results themselves and more in developing patience, curiosity, and the confidence to tackle unfamiliar problems.
